report:
(Fictional case study for training. Not a real investigation.)

Synopsis

On 7 July 2026 MV Tarrakin Star, a 24.4 m catamaran passenger ferry certificated for 96 passengers, made contact with Boolarong Bank at 6.8 kt over the ground at 18:12:04 while inbound from Muntari Island on service TF18 with 38 passengers and three crew (all times are local time, UTC+10). It came to rest heeled 4 degrees to starboard, 74 m west of the charted centreline of the Merrandi Channel and 54 m outside the dredged channel, on a falling tide in darkness. There were nil serious injuries. One passenger reported a grazed shin and two were treated at the wharf for distress. The starboard hull bottom plating was set up over 4.1 m with a 180 mm split in way of the No. 2 void, which flooded to approximately 260 mm, and the starboard propeller, shaft, rudder stock and skeg were damaged. The vessel refloated at 00:20 and the channel was closed to commercial traffic for 19 hours.

The chart plotter display froze at 18:07:06 and did not recover, and the master had no position fix of any kind from then. In the same second the heading began to ease from 195 to 200 degrees and was held there without a decision to turn, and the vessel set west, crossing the dredged channel's western edge at about 18:09:00. The master continued at about eight knots looking for the No. 4 beacon, which mangroves on Merrandi Islet screened where the vessel left the channel. The shallow alarm, still at its 2019 setting of 0.9 m under the keel, sounded at 18:11:48 and gave 16 seconds' warning against a 92 m crash stop.

The freeze, the heading change, the continued transit, the departure from the channel and the alarm setting were causal factors. The continued transit was very likely to have turned the loss of the plotter into a grounding, because a stop begun before about 18:11:40 would have halted the vessel short of the bank. The sightline clearing was deferred, unfunded, for three works rounds, and the screening was likely to have contributed to the heading change going unnoticed. The last service was moved into darkness without reopening the daylight-only route risk assessment, which was likely to have contributed to there being no night passage plan or hold point, and that absence very likely contributed to the transit continuing. The defect procedure did not require a self-cleared fault to be recorded, and was likely to have contributed to the fault remaining unaddressed. Whether the boat ramp floodlights delayed the beacon's sighting and whether the master was fatigued could not be determined.

The canopy trimming was completed on 24 July 2026 and a three-yearly cycle has been programmed. A local notice on the beacon's reduced range has been issued and Tarrakin Ferries has reissued its passage plan appendix. The Investigator in charge recommended a sightline test in place of the vegetation scope of the services agreement, and a night passage plan with a hold point from Tarrakin Ferries.

Factual information

History of the occurrence

The outgoing master had worked the morning shift on MV Tarrakin Star and handed over to the master at the town wharf at about 13:05. The chart plotter's event log shows two display freezes that morning, at 10:42 and 11:17, each with cause code 0x51, and the unit recovered itself both times. The outgoing master told the master about both freezes at the handover, and the master replied that the plotter had done the same to the master the month before. Neither entered the freezes in the wheelhouse defect book, and no entry of any kind was made for 7 July 2026 before the occurrence. The master then made two round trips before the last service of the day, TF18.

TF18 departed Muntari Island at 17:35:02 and the master reported the departure to Kanooka Heads Port Control on VHF channel 12 with 38 passengers. Port Control replied that there was nothing to affect the vessel and that the channel was clear. Sunset was at 17:02 and the end of civil twilight at 17:29. The service had been moved to this time under the winter timetable from 1 June 2026, so the transit was made in darkness. It was the thirty-first darkness run of TF18, which does not run on Sundays or public holidays. The three crew were the master, a deckhand and a kiosk attendant.

The vessel entered the Merrandi Channel from the north at 18:03:58, abeam the No. 1 beacon, 2 m east of the charted centreline and 1.13 nm north of the No. 4 beacon. Speed over the ground was 8.4 kt and course over the ground 195 degrees. At 18:04:10 the deckhand asked whether to stay on the bridge, and at 18:04:14 the master answered: "Nah, go and do the fares, I'll give you a yell coming up on the wharf." The deckhand left the bridge, and no other lookout was on the bridge afterwards. The vessel was abeam the No. 2 beacon at 18:05:30, 1 m west of the centreline, 0.90 nm north of the No. 4 beacon, still at 8.4 kt on 195 degrees.

The plotter's event log records the display process not responding at 18:07:06, with cause code 0x51 and no reset. The vessel was then 3 m west of the centreline and 0.68 nm north of the No. 4 beacon. The master said that the chart picture stayed on the screen with the vessel symbol stationary and that the display did not respond to touch. The audio has the master saying "Oh, come on" at 18:07:11, sounds consistent with repeated screen taps at 18:07:26, and the master saying "(unintelligible) frozen again" at 18:07:44.

From 18:07:06 the heading increased from 195 to 200 degrees over about a minute and was then held. The recorded rate of turn peaked at 6 degrees per minute at 18:07:40 and returned to zero by 18:08:50. The vessel moved west at about 20 m per minute once the new heading was held. No throttle movement was recorded. Speed over the ground was 8.1 kt at 18:08:00 and the vessel was 7 m west of the centreline.

At 18:08:31 the master said "Right. Where's four", when the vessel was 12 m west of the centreline and 0.47 nm north of the No. 4 beacon. At 18:09:00 the vessel was 20 m west of the centreline, which is the western edge of the dredged channel, 0.40 nm north of the beacon, at 8.0 kt. The audio has sounds consistent with a window or door being slid open at 18:09:40. At 18:10:02 the master said, to themselves, "There's four. Bring her back." The vessel was then 39 m west of the centreline, outside the dredged channel, 0.25 nm north of the beacon, at 7.9 kt with course over the ground 200 degrees. After that the course over the ground eased from 200 to 197 degrees, which slowed the westing without stopping it, and stayed west of the channel's 195 degrees until contact.

The vessel was 58 m west of the centreline and over Boolarong Bank at 18:11:00, at 7.6 kt. The echo sounder shallow alarm began at 18:11:48 with the vessel 70 m west of the centreline at 7.1 kt, and the master said "No no no" two seconds later. At 18:11:52 both throttles moved to astern together. The vessel made contact with the bank at 18:12:04 at 6.8 kt, 74 m west of the charted centreline and abeam the No. 4 beacon. The audio records a heavy impact followed by grinding and vibration for about 9 seconds. The vessel stopped within 11 m and came to rest heeled 4 degrees to starboard on a falling tide. The master operated the engine stop controls at 18:12:31 and the engines were not restarted.

At 18:12:16 the kiosk attendant asked, in a partly unintelligible remark, whether everyone was all right. At 18:12:40 the master addressed the passengers over the public address system. At 18:13:04 the master broadcast a pan pan on VHF channel 16 reporting the vessel aground on Boolarong Bank abeam the No. 4 beacon, 38 passengers and three crew, no injuries reported and no pollution. The master added: "Vessel is stable, we are upright, I am not attempting to refloat." Port Control acknowledged at 18:13:29, called the port workboat and asked the master to confirm that the vessel was not taking water. At 18:13:47 the master replied that the deckhand was sounding the voids and that the tide was falling.

The master addressed the passengers again at 18:14:52 and said that lifejackets were being handed out. At 18:16:20 the deckhand reported water in the No. 2 void, "Two, maybe three inches on the sounding rod", and the master directed that it be sounded every ten minutes. At 18:17:05 the master told Port Control that the ingress into the No. 2 starboard void was approximately 75 mm and that there was no ingress elsewhere. At 18:22:40 the deckhand reported that everyone was in a jacket, and said that for two passengers in the forward saloon the deckhand "had to go round the servery" because the locker was behind the counter with people standing at it. The port workboat came alongside the port quarter at 18:41:15. At 19:26:08 the master reported all 38 passengers ashore, with the crew of three remaining on board.

The vessel was refloated on the rising tide at 00:20 on 8 July 2026 and towed to the town wharf, where a starboard hull breach and progressive flooding of the No. 2 void were confirmed. The Merrandi Channel was closed to commercial traffic for 19 hours.

Injuries to persons

There were nil serious injuries. One passenger reported a grazed shin and two passengers were treated at the wharf for distress.

Recorded information

The shore AIS receiver log and the vessel's recorder readout give the track, speed, course and engine and steering parameters. They place the vessel on the charted centreline abeam the No. 2 beacon and show the offset to the west growing from 18:07:06. Speed over the ground fell from 8.4 kt to 7.6 kt between 18:07 and 18:11, with no throttle movement recorded until 18:11:52.

The engine monitoring recorder shows both engines at 1,780 and 1,784 rpm, within 12 rpm of each other, from 18:03 to 18:11:52, with no alarm and no temperature or pressure excursion. Steering gear hydraulic pressure was 96 to 99 bar throughout, against a normal band of 90 to 105 bar. Rudder angle followed helm demand within 1.5 degrees. At 18:11:52 both throttles moved to the astern detent together, and astern thrust was developing but had not reached full at the moment of contact.

The plotter's internal event log shows watchdog resets with cause code 0x51 at 10:42 and 11:17 on 7 July 2026, the display process not responding at 18:07:06 with no reset, and power removed at 18:16.

The echo sounder log shows the shallow alarm set to 0.9 m under the keel. It sounded once on the voyage, at 18:11:48, and the tone continued to 18:12:20. The log gives the distance covered in the 16 seconds to contact as 58 m at 7.1 kt.

The audio comes from the Port Control VHF channel 12 and 16 recordings and the bridge camera, covering 17:32 to 19:26. It was transcribed on 16 July 2026 and verified by the Port Authority's traffic officer. The bridge audio contains no remark about the steering or the engines at any point.

Equipment information

MV Tarrakin Star is a 24.4 m aluminium catamaran passenger ferry certificated for 96 passengers, with a beam of 8.2 m. The vessel completed its annual survey on 11 March 2026 with no outstanding conditions, and its last slipping was in March 2025. Its static draught was 1.35 m and the calculated squat at 6.8 kt was 0.18 m. The vessel's own trials figure for a crash stop from 8 kt is 92 m. [NOT ESTABLISHED: the vessel's builder, year of build and registration or other identifier]

The chart plotter is a 12-inch multifunction display fed by a separate GPS antenna unit, running chart software revision 4.11 on firmware issued in March 2024. The echo sounder's shallow alarm was set to 0.9 m under the keel when the unit was commissioned in 2019 and had not been changed. The vessel carries 120 adult and 20 child lifejackets in four lockers. The forward saloon locker holds 40 adult jackets and the forward saloon has 34 seats.

The wheelhouse defect book had eleven entries in the 90 days before the occurrence. None concerned the chart plotter, the GPS antenna, the echo sounder, the steering gear, the engines or the propulsion controls. The open items on 7 July 2026 were a seized port aft mooring bollard cover, a saloon window seal weeping and a defective deck light on the aft boarding gate. The maintenance system held no work order, fault report or correspondence about the chart plotter at any time in 2026. The firmware bulletin that the electronics contractor later identified, issued in November 2024 and addressing cause code 0x51, was not held by the operator, which had no subscription to the manufacturer's bulletins.

Damage

The post-grounding survey, carried out between 9 and 14 July 2026, found the following.

  • Starboard hull bottom plating was set up over 4.1 m between frames 6 and 11, with a 180 mm split on the centreline of the hull in way of the No. 2 void.
  • Ingress into the No. 2 void was approximately 75 mm at 18:16 and approximately 260 mm when the vessel refloated at 00:20.
  • All three starboard propeller blades were bent aft with distorted tips, the shaft was bent 1.4 mm over its length, and the stern gland was undamaged.
  • The starboard rudder stock was distorted 3 degrees, and the starboard skeg was torn away and recovered from the bank on 8 July 2026.
  • No damage was found to the port hull, propulsion or steering.

Meteorology

The Kanooka Heads weather station recorded wind from 310 degrees at 9 kt at 17:30, 305 degrees at 8 kt at 18:00 and 310 degrees at 7 kt at 18:30. Visibility was over 10 km throughout. Cloud was FEW at 3,500 ft at 17:30 and 18:00 and SCT at 3,500 ft at 18:30. Temperature was 14 degrees at 17:30 and 13 degrees at 18:00 and 18:30, pressure was 1021 hPa and then 1022 hPa, and no rain fell after 09:00. The port workboat reported the sea state in the channel at 18:45 as slight, with wind ripple only and no swell penetrating the entrance.

Sunset was at 17:02 and the end of civil twilight at 17:29. Moonrise was at 06:12, with the waning crescent 2% illuminated.

Predicted high water at the Kanooka River entrance was 15:20 at 1.66 m above chart datum and predicted low water was 21:34 at 0.30 m. The predicted height at 18:12 was 0.94 m. The Port Authority gauge at Kanooka Heads read 0.99 m at 18:00, 0.91 m at 18:12 and 0.79 m at 18:30. The gauge's largest departure from prediction in the 12 hours to 20:00 was 0.07 m, at 11:40. The surveyed bed level at the contact point was 0.50 m below chart datum, so the water over it at 18:12 was 1.41 m.

Site information

The Merrandi Channel is a dredged recreational and commercial access channel on a waterway managed by Kanooka Shire Council through the Kanooka Heads Port Authority. It is not a declared shipping channel. It is 40 m wide and dredged to 3.2 m, with six beacons. Boolarong Bank lies to the west of the channel and dries in places. The surveyed gradient of the bank across the contact section was about 1 in 70.

The grounding position was surveyed on 8 July 2026 at 74 m west of the charted centreline. That is 54 m west of the channel's western edge and 34 m west of the No. 4 beacon. The bed level was 0.50 m below chart datum at the contact point, rising to 0.15 m below datum 30 m further west. Furrows consistent with the starboard hull and skeg ran 11 m from the point of first contact on a heading of 197 degrees.

The operator's passage plan lists the aids as the No. 1 beacon (Fl G 4s, range 4 M), the No. 2 beacon (Fl R 4s, range 4 M), the No. 4 beacon (Fl G 2.5s, range 6 M) and the No. 6 beacon (Fl R 2.5s, range 4 M). The town wharf leading lights bear 195 degrees and lie about 1.9 nm beyond the No. 6 beacon. They do not resolve as two lights until the vessel is inside the channel's southern third.

The Port Authority's register shows the following about the No. 4 beacon.

  • The beacon was converted from a mains supply to a solar lantern in November 2025 under the Council's waterways energy programme.
  • The replacement lantern is rated at a nominal range of 3 nm against 6 nm for the lantern it replaced. The character, Fl G 2.5s, did not change, and the lantern is 4.2 m above chart datum.
  • A notification was lodged with the hydrographic service on 4 February 2026 and the chart correction was still pending on 7 July 2026. No local notice to mariners was issued, and no operator using the channel was told.
  • Work order WO-118, raised in September 2023, described mangrove regrowth on Merrandi Islet screening the beacon from the northern approach between about half a mile and a quarter mile. It recommended trimming to 2 m on a three-yearly cycle at an estimated $18,500, and was deferred at the 2023, 2024 and 2025 works rounds, each entry reading "defer, unfunded, refer next round".
  • Work order WO-176, raised in March 2026, described the same sightline as "now fully closed on the northern approach". The Authority's file note against it states that the islet is 240 m from the beacon, which is outside the 50 m scope of schedule 2.4 of the services agreement, and that the work therefore competes with boat ramps and pontoons in the general waterways vote.
  • The beacon was recorded as "observed, operating" on the monthly check in every month from January 2024 to July 2026, the last on 2 July 2026. The check is made from the town wharf, 2.1 nm south of the beacon, from which Merrandi Islet is not in the line of sight.
  • No defect has been recorded against the beacon and no notice about it has been issued to a waterway user.

A range and visibility check on 18 July 2026, made at the investigator's request from the port workboat on the inbound track at the same time of night, measured the lantern's luminous range at 2.6 nm. The light was not visible at all from the channel between 0.84 nm and 0.34 nm north of the beacon. Over that stretch the sightline passes through the mangrove canopy on Merrandi Islet, about 240 m north of the beacon in the shoal strip between the dredged western edge and the bank, and about 10 m across. Beyond 0.84 nm the sightline passes west of the islet and inside 0.34 nm it passes east of it. The canopy measured 5.8 m, against 2.1 m in the aerial survey flown for the Council in 2019. The check was made on the inbound track, and a vessel west of that track sees the light open earlier. The vessel on 7 July 2026 passed about 24 m west of the islet at about 18:11.

A foreshore lighting survey on 18 July 2026 covered the Kanooka Heads foreshore redevelopment, commissioned on 22 May 2026, ten days before the winter timetable began. It includes 14 LED floodlights on 12 m columns lighting the new boat ramp and car park, 300 m east of the town wharf. Measured from the inbound track, each floodlight presents about 4,800 candela toward the channel and none is shielded to seaward. From 0.5 nm north of the No. 4 beacon the array lies behind the beacon within 4 degrees of the same bearing and within 1.5 degrees of the same elevation. The array is continuously lit, while the beacon flashes green for 0.4 seconds every 2.5 seconds. The Council's planning unit approved the redevelopment. The Port Authority's aids to navigation officer was not consulted, and no assessment of the lighting against the channel's aids was carried out or required.

Personnel information

The master held a master's certificate for sheltered-waters passenger vessels, held since 2012. The master had 14 years as a master, 11 with Tarrakin Ferries and all 11 on the Muntari Island route, and about 19 years in commercial marine operations. The master had made approximately 4,100 transits of the Merrandi Channel. The last route check was on 14 February 2026 and was satisfactory, and there was no prior occurrence history. Of the 30 darkness transits of the channel between 1 June 2026 and the occurrence, the master had made 26.

The route is worked on a cycle of 12 days on and 2 days off, and 7 July 2026 was the master's ninth consecutive day. The day's duty was a split, 05:40 to 08:40 on another of the operator's three vessels and 13:00 to 19:20 on MV Tarrakin Star. That is 9 hours 20 minutes of duty across a spread of 13 hours 40 minutes, with a 4 hour 20 minute unpaid break at home. Both figures are inside the operator's limits of 10 hours of duty and 14 hours of spread, and inside the crewing determination that applies to the route. The master recorded 6 hours 15 minutes of sleep on the night of 6 July in the fatigue diary that the operator asks masters to keep but does not collect.

The outgoing master held a master's certificate for sheltered-waters passenger vessels. The outgoing master had 9 years as a master, 6 with Tarrakin Ferries and 4 on the route, about 15 years in commercial marine operations and approximately 1,400 transits of the channel. The last route check was on 9 November 2025 and was satisfactory. The outgoing master worked 05:40 to 13:05 on 7 July 2026, on day six of a twelve-day tour, and had made the other 4 of the 30 darkness transits before the occurrence.

The deckhand had been with the operator for 7 months and held a basic marine safety certificate and a coxswain's certificate. It was the deckhand's first winter season on the route. [NOT ESTABLISHED: the kiosk attendant's qualifications, experience and account]

Organisational and management information

Passage planning

The operator's Operations Manual OPS-3 (revision 6, February 2023) provided as follows.

  • "3.2 A written passage plan is held for each scheduled route. The master will conduct the passage in accordance with the plan and will record any departure from it in the deck log." (OPS-3)
  • "3.4 The Merrandi Channel transit will be made on the charted centreline, monitored on the chart plotter, with the No. 2 and No. 4 beacons identified visually before the vessel passes the No. 1 beacon." (OPS-3)
  • "3.6 In reduced visibility the master will reduce to a speed at which the vessel can be stopped within the distance in which the channel can be seen, and will consider anchoring or returning to open water." (OPS-3)

Appendix A, the Merrandi Channel passage plan, is issue 2 of February 2023 and is the current issue. It gives a transit speed of 8 knots, a course of 195 degrees true inbound, the chart plotter as the primary means of position fixing, and the visual transit of the No. 4 beacon with the town wharf leading lights as the secondary means. It lists Boolarong Bank to the west of the channel, drying, and a minimum depth of 3.2 m below datum. It ends: "Note: this plan is written for the daylight transit. Night transits are not scheduled on this route." It records the No. 4 beacon at 6 M.

There is no night passage plan for the Merrandi Channel. The plan contains no guidance on what to do if the plotter is lost during the transit and names no abort or hold point. OPS-3 does not address whether a lookout should be on the bridge during the channel transit.

Route risk assessment and the timetable change

Route Risk Assessment RRA-07 issue 2 (March 2023) is the current assessment for the channel and no issue 3 exists. It assessed these hazards: Boolarong Bank to the west of the channel, a channel width of 40 m against a vessel beam of 8.2 m, a single unlit reach between the No. 2 and No. 4 beacons, a tidal range of 1.4 m, and recreational traffic at weekends. Its controls were transit at 8 knots on the charted centreline, the chart plotter monitored throughout, and the No. 4 beacon identified before passing No. 1. Its operating restriction read: "daylight transits only. A night transit of the Merrandi Channel requires the General Manager Operations' approval and a specific passage plan."

Change record CHG-2026-014, "Winter timetable, Muntari Island route", moved TF18 from 16:15 to 17:35 from 1 June to 31 August 2026 to meet the afternoon coach connection at the town wharf. It assessed the change as "timetable change only", recorded "No new hazard identified" and answered "No" to route risk assessment review required. The Operations Manager approved it on 22 April 2026. The change record does not refer to the daylight-only restriction. RRA-07 was not reopened and no night passage plan was written. The General Manager Operations' approval was neither sought nor given. Between 1 June 2026 and the occurrence TF18 ran 31 times in darkness, the occurrence transit being the thirty-first.

Defect reporting

The operator's Operations Manual OPS-9 (revision 4, August 2024) provided as follows.

  • "9.1 A defect which renders the vessel unseaworthy or which affects a statutory item of equipment shall be reported to the Operations Manager immediately and entered in the vessel defect book." (OPS-9)
  • "9.2 All other defects shall be entered in the vessel defect book at the end of the shift in which they are found, and will be reviewed by the Operations Manager weekly." (OPS-9)
  • "9.3 At a change of master the outgoing master will brief the relieving master on the state of the vessel, any defect, and anything else affecting the conduct of the service." (OPS-9)

OPS-9 does not require the change-of-master brief to be written down, and does not require the relieving master to confirm that a defect mentioned in it has been entered in the defect book. The defect book is a bound book kept in the wheelhouse and is transcribed into the maintenance system when the Operations Manager reviews it. The chart plotter is not a statutory item on a sheltered-waters passenger vessel on this route, and it is the primary means of position fixing named in the passage plan. The company reporting system has a "navigation hazard" category. It had not been used on this route in three years, and no master interviewed knew that it existed.

Rostering

Five masters work the Muntari Island route, all on the same cycle of 12 days on and 2 days off. In the winter timetable TF18 closes the afternoon half of a split duty, 05:40 to 08:40 and 13:00 to 19:20, and the master on that line works the same split on every day of the tour, days nine to twelve included. The darkness transit of the channel therefore falls in the last hour and a quarter of a 13 hour 40 minute spread, which ends 20 minutes inside the operator's 14 hour limit. No relief master is rostered, and a master who reports unfit is covered by extending another master's tour.

External requirements and agreements

The Waterways Aids to Navigation Code WAN-2 section 4 provided as follows.

  • "4.1 The authority responsible for an aid to navigation must maintain it so that it performs the function for which it was established." (WAN-2)
  • "4.2 Where an aid to navigation is established on a declared shipping channel, the responsible authority must record its availability, must achieve an availability of not less than 99.0 per cent measured annually, and must notify a change to the aid's character, position or range by notice to mariners before the change takes effect." (WAN-2)
  • "4.3 Where an aid to navigation is established on a waterway that is not a declared shipping channel, section 4.2 does not apply. The responsible authority must be able to demonstrate that the aid is inspected at intervals it has determined and recorded." (WAN-2)

Section 4.2 therefore does not apply to any of the Merrandi Channel's six beacons. The code does not define the function at 4.1. The Authority reads it as lit, on station and showing its charted character, which is what its register shows.

Schedule 2 of the services agreement between Kanooka Shire Council and the Kanooka Heads Port Authority provided as follows.

  • "S2.1 The Authority will inspect each lit aid by daylight once per quarter and will confirm each lit aid's operation by observation from the town wharf once per month." (services agreement, schedule 2)
  • "S2.4 Vegetation management within 50 m of an aid is a works item and is funded from the general waterways maintenance vote. Vegetation beyond 50 m is not within the scope of this agreement." (services agreement, schedule 2)
  • "S2.7 Defects found are recorded in the aids to navigation register and actioned in accordance with the Authority's maintenance priority scale. There is no requirement in this agreement to notify waterway users of a defect, a deferral or a change to an aid." (services agreement, schedule 2)

Nothing in the agreement requires any aid to be observed from the approach a vessel actually uses. When asked on 20 July 2026, the Port Authority said that no operator had asked about the channel's aids and that the aids to navigation register had not been provided to Tarrakin Ferries.

Tests and research

The plotter was bench tested by an approved electronics contractor on 21 July 2026 over 46 hours, with the same antenna and cabling. The fault did not recur and no defect was found. The contractor reported that cause code 0x51 is known to the manufacturer and is addressed by firmware issued in November 2024, which had not been applied to this unit.

The whole steering system was examined on 12 July 2026. Both rams, the tiller arms, the hydraulic system and the autopilot were removed and function tested. All were serviceable, with no internal leakage, no air in the system and no sign of a pre-existing defect. The system passed a full lock-to-lock timing test inside the specified period.

The grounding position survey, the range and visibility check and the foreshore lighting survey are described under Site information.

Other information

Survival and emergency response

The forward saloon lifejacket locker is mounted in the bulkhead behind the kiosk servery counter. The counter was fitted during a 2019 interior refit carried out under a minor modification notice, which did not trigger a re-survey of the safety equipment arrangement. The arrangement approved at build in 2011 had an open bench in that position with the locker face clear. A stowage survey on 16 July 2026 found that the locker face cannot be reached from 22 of the 34 forward saloon seats without passing behind the counter through a 0.6 m gap at its inboard end. With three people standing at the counter, as there were on the night, that gap is the only route. The muster placard in the forward saloon directs passengers to "the locker forward on the port side", which is the locker in question and is not visible from the seats. The operator said that the same counter is fitted to its two other 24 m vessels.

All 38 passengers were in lifejackets by about 18:22. The first passengers were addressed within 36 seconds of the impact. The No. 2 starboard void was sounded from 18:16 and every ten minutes after. The last passenger was ashore at 19:26.

Accounts

The master was interviewed and described the transit in these terms. The plotter froze after the vessel passed the No. 2 beacon. The master tried it twice, then went looking for the No. 4 beacon out of the window. The master said: "You're looking into a wall of light." The master said of the heading: "I eased her to starboard while I was fiddling with the plotter and then looking for four. Five degrees. I never made that decision." When the beacon was found dead ahead, the master said the vessel was off the line to the west and that both throttles went astern straight away once the alarm sounded. The master said the beacon appeared dead ahead and not out on the starboard bow, where it belongs.

Asked whether stopping was considered when the plotter froze, the master said: "No. And that's the honest answer and it's not a good one. I didn't think about it. I went straight to the visual transit because in my head the visual transit is the backup. There's nothing that tells you to stop." On seeing the beacon, the master said: "I brought her back to port to get in again. I thought I was just outside the edge, a boat width maybe, so a few degrees and I'd be back on the line." The master added: "I was nearly forty metres out."

On the handover and the defect book, the master said: "The book is for things that are broken when you hand over. If it's broken you write it, if it came good you say it." On the beacon, the master said it had become harder to see over two years and had been mentioned to other masters and the workboat crew but never reported, because "There's no form for the beacon looks dim. It's not our beacon. And I don't know who'd read it." On the timetable change, the master said only a new roster sheet came with it, with no brief or plan. On the master's own state, the master said: "I was tired. I'd be lying if I said otherwise." The master also said: "But I wasn't fighting to stay awake and I wasn't slow." The master gave the reasons for not refloating as the falling tide, an unknown bottom, 38 people on board and the grinding heard for about nine seconds, and said: "On the bank she can't sink."

The outgoing master was interviewed by telephone. The outgoing master recalled that the plotter froze first on the 10:20 departure from the town wharf, about twenty minutes in, and again on the 11:05 return. Both freezes were in open water outside the channel, and the display recovered itself after a minute or two. The plotter's event log records the two freezes at 10:42 and 11:17. The outgoing master said that neither freeze was in the Merrandi Channel and that a freeze there would have been treated very differently. The outgoing master told the master about both at the handover. The outgoing master did not enter them in the defect book, said that no one had asked for it, and did not think of them as defects because the display had recovered.

Asked what would have been done had the plotter frozen inside the channel, the outgoing master said the way would have been taken off the vessel until the display recovered or the position was confirmed on the marks, because there is no traffic and nothing to hit when stopped. The outgoing master knew of no rule requiring this. The outgoing master believed the plotter had frozen three or four times on this vessel in the past year, to the outgoing master and to others, and that none had been written up. The outgoing master said the No. 4 beacon had been "going backwards" for two years and was hard work at night, and had become washed out from the northern approach since the car park lighting went in. The outgoing master had mentioned this to the workboat crew a couple of times and had never reported it, as there was no form and it was the council's light. Only a new roster accompanied the timetable change.

In the master's safety report, submitted on the evening of the occurrence, the master described the plotter freezing and being told of the earlier freezes at the changeover. The master wrote of continuing at eight knots and looking for the beacon for about a minute and a half. The master described the light behind the beacon and the weak flash in front of it. The master reported putting the vessel five degrees to starboard without deciding to, then easing back to port on seeing the beacon, believing the vessel to be just outside the edge. The master reported both throttles astern within a few seconds of the alarm, stopping the engines, not attempting to back off, and the actions that followed. The master reported that no night plan had been provided, that nothing but the departure time changed when the timetable moved into darkness, and that there was no place to report the beacon's condition.

The deckhand's safety report, submitted on 10 July 2026, described issuing lifejackets from the aft saloon forward. The aft saloon locker is on the bulkhead and passengers opened it themselves. In the forward saloon the deckhand had to ask three people standing at the counter to move, go round the end of the counter through a narrow gap and hand jackets out over the counter one at a time. The deckhand reported that this took a couple of minutes, that passengers were calm, and that the placard points to a locker not visible from the seats. The deckhand believed the arrangement was the same on the operator's other two vessels.

Analysis

Scope of the analysis

The analysis has to settle why a serviceable vessel with a qualified and experienced master left a 40 m wide dredged channel in calm conditions and grounded 54 m outside it, and why the defences available did not prevent it. It follows the sequence from the plotter freeze and the organisational conditions behind it to the grounding, then deals with two matters that could not be settled and with factors that did not influence the occurrence. In this style a causal factor is one without which the occurrence would not have happened, and a contributory factor made it more likely or its outcome worse without being essential to it.

The evidence excluded several conditions. The master held a master's certificate for sheltered-waters passenger vessels since 2012, had about 4,100 transits of the channel and had passed a route check on 14 February 2026. The master had no prior occurrence history. The vessel completed its annual survey on 11 March 2026 with no outstanding conditions. The engine recorder showed both engines at 1,780 and 1,784 rpm with no alarm. Steering gear hydraulic pressure held at 96 to 99 bar and rudder angle followed helm demand within 1.5 degrees. The steering system, removed and tested on 12 July 2026, was serviceable in every component. The weather was not a factor. The wind was offshore at 8 to 9 kt, visibility exceeded 10 km and the sea in the channel was slight. Darkness was a condition of the transit rather than a fault, because civil twilight ended at 17:29 and the moon was a waning crescent 2% illuminated, so every reference available to the master was an artificial light. The tide was not a factor, as set out at the end of this analysis.

The frozen plotter and the missing defence against it

The Merrandi Channel passage plan made the chart plotter the primary means of position fixing. It named as the secondary means the visual transit of the No. 4 beacon with the town wharf leading lights. The leading lights bear 195 degrees but lie about 1.9 nm beyond the No. 6 beacon and do not resolve as two lights until the vessel is inside the channel's southern third. When the plotter stopped, 0.68 nm north of the No. 4 beacon, the secondary means was therefore the beacon alone.

Until then the transit went as the plan intended. The vessel entered the channel at 18:03:58 at 8.4 kt, 2 m east of the centreline, and was 1 m west of it abeam the No. 2 beacon at 18:05:30. It was 3 m west at 18:07:06, and helm work held the centreline to within 3 m for the first two minutes in the channel. The plotter's event log then records the display process not responding at 18:07:06 with no reset, under cause code 0x51, the code it had logged and recovered from at 10:42 and 11:17 that morning. The bridge audio agrees with the log. "Oh, come on" was recorded at 18:07:11, repeated screen taps at 18:07:26 and "(unintelligible) frozen again" at 18:07:44. The master described the chart picture staying on the screen with the vessel symbol stationary and the display not accepting touch.

A 46 hour bench test on 21 July 2026 with the same antenna and cabling did not reproduce the fault and found no physical defect, so the test did not show directly what caused this freeze. The contractor identified cause code 0x51 as known to the manufacturer and addressed by firmware issued in November 2024, which the unit, running firmware issued in March 2024, had never had applied. The loss of the plotter left the master with no means of fixing the vessel's position from 18:07:06 until the beacon was sighted at 18:10:02. It is extremely likely that this loss influenced both the heading change and the continuation of the transit that followed. The Investigation concluded that the freeze was a causal factor.

Why the fault was still in the unit

The operator's defect procedure required immediate reporting only of a defect that rendered the vessel unseaworthy or affected a statutory item. The chart plotter is not a statutory item on this vessel on this route, although it was the primary means of position fixing in the passage plan. OPS-9 9.2 required all other defects to be "entered in the vessel defect book at the end of the shift in which they are found", for weekly review by the Operations Manager. For a fault that had come and gone before the shift ended, that provision was no trigger at all, and the manual does not say whether such a fault is a defect. OPS-9 9.3 required the outgoing master to brief the relieving master on "any defect", but nothing required the brief to be written down or the relieving master to check afterwards that a defect was booked.

Both masters read the procedure the same way, independently. The master said "The book is for things that are broken when you hand over. If it's broken you write it, if it came good you say it." The book's eleven entries in the 90 days before the occurrence were all faults present when they were written, and none concerned the plotter. The outgoing master said the plotter had frozen three or four times on this vessel in the previous year and that none had been written up. It had also frozen on the relieving master a month earlier. The maintenance system held no work order, fault report or correspondence about the plotter in 2026. The operator held no subscription to the manufacturer's bulletins, so the firmware that addressed the cause code did not reach the vessel.

There is contrary evidence. A recorded freeze would have had to pass through the Operations Manager's weekly review and then to somebody ashore who found the manufacturer's bulletin. The operator had no subscription to the bulletins, so a recorded freeze might have been reviewed at the end of the week, noted and left. Nothing shows how many recorded freezes it would have taken to send the unit to the contractor, or how quickly. That uncertainty goes to speed rather than to whether, because a year of freezes on the primary means of position fixing is unlikely to have reached nobody, and a single bench test was enough for the contractor to name the fix. It is likely that the procedure's failure to require a self-cleared fault to be recorded contributed to the freeze at 18:07:06, because no freeze ever reached a place where the fix could have been found. The Investigation concluded that this was a causal factor.

The fault passed on at the handover

The plotter's log shows two freezes on the morning shift, at 10:42 and 11:17, from which the unit recovered itself. The outgoing master told the relieving master of both at about 13:05 at the town wharf. The relieving master replied that it had done the same a month earlier. The outgoing master said both freezes occurred outside the Merrandi Channel and that a freeze inside it would have been thought about very differently. Neither entered the freezes in the defect book, no entry of any kind was made for 7 July 2026 before the occurrence, and both masters volunteered the omission before they were asked about it.

This did not influence the occurrence. A defect book entry at about 13:05 would have gone to the Operations Manager's weekly review, and nothing written that afternoon could have applied firmware to the unit or taken the vessel off service TF18 by 18:07. The omission matters because it was the practice and not a lapse. Both masters described the same rule, and it is the visible instance of the procedure gap described above. It is likely to carry importance as a standing risk, and the Investigation treated it as a contributory factor that increased risk without having influenced this occurrence.

The transit continuing at about eight knots

OPS-3 3.6 required, "In reduced visibility", a speed at which the vessel could be stopped within the distance the channel could be seen, and consideration of anchoring or returning to open water. Visibility exceeded 10 km, so the provision did not apply, and no other provision addressed the loss of the plotter.

The AIS track records no reduction of speed after the freeze. Speed was 8.4 kt at 18:07:06 and 8.1 kt at 18:08:00. It fell to 7.1 kt by 18:11:48 through shoaling drag, with no throttle movement on the engine recorder until 18:11:52. The master's attention moved to the search for the beacon at 18:08:31, 85 seconds after the freeze. The master said stopping did not cross the mind and that the visual transit was taken to be the backup. The vessel crossed the channel's western edge about 114 seconds after the freeze. A crash stop from 8 kt needed 92 m according to the vessel's own trials, there was no other traffic, the water was flat, and the wind was offshore at 8 kt. Stopping was therefore available from the freeze until about 18:11:40. On the evidence, a stop in the first 114 seconds would have left the vessel in the channel, and a stop after the sighting would have left it on the bank's margin, upright and not holed.

The master's account of why the vessel was not stopped after the sighting was this. At 18:10:02 the master saw the beacon dead ahead and knew the vessel was off the line to the west. The master judged the vessel to be just outside the edge, "a boat width maybe", and eased back to port, and said "Stopping right there, on the edge of a bank I couldn't see, felt worse than easing her back in." The vessel was 39 m west of the centreline. The course over ground came back from 200 to 197 degrees, still west of the channel's 195. The reasoning was sincere, but it rested on a misjudged position and could not outweigh a stop that cost nothing. Nothing in the 98 seconds from 18:10:02 stopped the vessel being slowed.

The outgoing master said the answer to a freeze inside the channel would have been to take the way off and sit there, because nothing could be hit while stopped. The outgoing master said there was no rule requiring it and that it was "just what you'd do". No lookout was on the bridge, because the deckhand had been sent to collect fares at 18:04:14. This is normal practice on the route and OPS-3 does not address it either way. It is extremely likely that continuing at about eight knots with no means of fixing the position turned the loss of the plotter into a grounding. The Investigation concluded that this was a causal factor.

No night passage plan or hold point

OPS-3 Appendix A, issue 2 and current, gives a transit speed, a course, a primary and a secondary means of fixing and the hazards. It closes with the note "this plan is written for the daylight transit. Night transits are not scheduled on this route." There was no night passage plan, no guidance on what to do if the plotter was lost during the transit, and no abort or hold point named anywhere in the plan. OPS-3 3.4 required the transit to be "monitored on the chart plotter" and said nothing of its loss.

The operator's own defence against this sequence was therefore never written. The master had 114 seconds between the freeze and crossing the channel edge, and a crash stop begun at any point before about 18:11:40 would have stopped the vessel short of the contact point. A named hold point would have applied throughout that period. Both masters said that stopping was the right answer and that nothing anywhere asks for it. A master who did not think of stopping unprompted might not have applied a written rule under the same pressure. That possibility does not remove the gap, because a rule written in advance is the means of supplying the thought the master did not have. It is very likely that the absence of a night passage plan and hold point influenced the continuation of the transit. The Investigation concluded that this was a causal factor.

Why the run was in darkness without that plan

RRA-07 issue 2 (March 2023) carried the operating restriction: "daylight transits only. A night transit of the Merrandi Channel requires the General Manager Operations' approval and a specific passage plan." It also named as a hazard the "single unlit reach between the No. 2 and No. 4 beacons".

Change record CHG-2026-014 moved service TF18 from 16:15 to 17:35 from 1 June 2026 to meet a coach connection. It assessed the change as "timetable change only", recorded "No new hazard identified" and answered "No" to whether a route risk assessment review was required. The Operations Manager approved it on 22 April 2026, one level below the person whose approval the restriction named. RRA-07 was not reopened, no issue 3 exists, no night passage plan was written, and the General Manager Operations' approval was neither sought nor given. TF18 then ran in darkness 31 times before the occurrence, which was the thirty-first. The master recalled that the change came with a new roster sheet and no brief, plan or conversation.

Had RRA-07 been reviewed against a night operation, the review would have reached the unlit reach it already named, and the restriction could not have been closed without a plan. A reopened assessment might nevertheless have produced a night plan that said no more than the daylight one, with no hold point, and the vessel would then have met the frozen plotter in the same way. The restriction named the plan, however, and a plan written for this channel was the document most likely to say what to do when the primary fix was lost. It is likely that the decision to move the last service into darkness without reopening the assessment contributed to there being no night plan or hold point. [NOT ESTABLISHED: why the change was assessed as a timetable change only, because the Operations Manager's account of what was understood the restriction to require has been given verbally and has not been taken as a formal interview.] The Investigation concluded that this was a causal factor.

The heading change and the vessel leaving the channel

From 18:07:06, the second the plotter froze, the heading increased steadily from 195 to 200 degrees over about a minute and was then held. The rate of turn peaked at 6 degrees per minute at 18:07:40, while the master was at the frozen screen, and was back to zero by 18:08:50. Rudder angle followed helm demand within 1.5 degrees, so the turn was steered. It was not a current or wind effect, because the wind was offshore at 8 kt and there was no cross-set in the channel at that state of tide.

The master's account was "I eased her to starboard while I was fiddling with the plotter and then looking for four. Five degrees. I never made that decision." Nothing on the bridge showed the new heading, because the plotter's vessel symbol was frozen and the beacon was screened. Held at 200 degrees against the channel's 195, the heading moved the vessel west at about 20 m a minute. The vessel reached the channel's western edge, 20 m from the centreline, at about 18:09:00, 0.40 nm north of the beacon. It was 39 m west at 18:10:02 and over Boolarong Bank from about 18:11:00. The heading change was virtually certain to have been the cause of the westing, and the grounding followed directly from the vessel being outside the dredged channel. The Investigation concluded that the heading change and the vessel's departure from the channel were causal factors.

The screening of the No. 4 beacon

A range and visibility check on 18 July 2026, made from the port workboat on the inbound track at the same time of night, found that the No. 4 beacon was not visible from the channel between 0.84 nm and 0.34 nm north of it. The sightline over that stretch passes through the mangrove canopy on Merrandi Islet, about 240 m up-channel of the beacon. The canopy measured 5.8 m against a lantern height of 4.2 m. The Port Authority's register had recorded the screening since September 2023 and described the sightline as "now fully closed on the northern approach" in March 2026.

With the plotter frozen, the beacon was the only means of fixing left. The audio records "Right. Where's four" at 18:08:31 and "There's four. Bring her back." at 18:10:02, 91 seconds apart. The vessel was 0.47 nm north of the beacon when the search began, crossed the channel's western edge at about 0.40 nm, inside the screened arc, and was 0.25 nm north when the beacon was called. Seen on the starboard bow where it belongs, the light would have shown the vessel drawing west within a minute of the turn, while it was still in the channel.

There is contrary evidence on two points. The heading change began at 18:07:06, before the search began, so the screening cannot have caused the turn and explains only why it went unnoticed. The check was also made from the inbound track, and a vessel west of the track sees the light open earlier. The beacon was clear of the islet for at least the last 37 seconds of the search, from about 18:09:25, and was still not seen. The first point limits the factor to the turn going unnoticed, which is how it is judged here. The second belongs to the floodlight question below and does not undo the screening over the preceding minute and a half. It is likely that the screening contributed to the heading change going unnoticed. The Investigation concluded that this was a causal factor.

The deferral behind the screening

Work order WO-118, raised in September 2023, recorded mangrove regrowth on Merrandi Islet screening the beacon from the northern approach between about half a mile and a quarter mile. It recommended trimming to 2 m on a three-yearly cycle at an estimated $18,500. It was deferred at the 2023, 2024 and 2025 works rounds, each entry reading "defer, unfunded, refer next round". The Authority's file note against WO-176, raised in March 2026, recorded that the islet is 240 m from the beacon and so outside the 50 m vegetation scope of schedule 2.4 of the services agreement, so that the work competed with boat ramps and pontoons in the general waterways vote. The monthly check that recorded the beacon "observed, operating" from January 2024 to July 2026 was made from the town wharf, 2.1 nm south of the beacon, from which the islet is not in the line of sight. No defect was ever recorded against the beacon, and neither master had ever reported its poor visibility. One master said there was no form and nobody to report it to.

The canopy measured 2.1 m in the 2019 aerial survey and 5.8 m in July 2026, about half a metre a year. A trim funded at the 2023 round would therefore have left it near 3.5 m on the night, under the 4.2 m lantern, and the beacon would have been open to the channel over the stretch where it was screened. [NOT ESTABLISHED: whether the canopy grew evenly between the 2019 and 2026 measurements, because the register gives those two measurements and the work order's description and nothing in between.] It is very likely that the deferral of the sightline work for three works rounds led to the screening. The Investigation concluded that this was a causal factor.

The shallow alarm

The echo sounder's shallow alarm was set to 0.9 m under the keel, the value written into the setup at commissioning in 2019 and never changed. It sounded at 18:11:48, and both throttles went astern together four seconds later at 18:11:52. Contact followed at 18:12:04 at 6.8 kt, 16 seconds after the alarm. At 7.1 kt the vessel covered 58 m in that time against the vessel's trials figure of 92 m for a crash stop from 8 kt. Astern thrust was developing but had not reached full at contact. On the surveyed bank gradient of about 1 in 70, the alarm could not have sounded appreciably earlier at that setting.

A setting of about 1.6 m under the keel would have sounded about 107 m short of the contact, enough for a crash stop with four seconds to react, and would still not have sounded in the dredged channel at low water. A setting that gave forty seconds' warning would sound within the dredged channel at low water, which is why the setting has to be chosen for the channel rather than simply raised. The equipment did exactly what it was set to do, and the finding concerns the setting and the speed. It is extremely likely that the setting, by giving warning that the vessel could not use, influenced the grounding. The Investigation concluded that this was a causal factor.

Unresolved: boat ramp floodlights behind the No. 4 beacon

The foreshore survey of 18 July 2026 found 14 unshielded LED floodlights on 12 m columns at the new boat ramp, each presenting about 4,800 candela toward the channel. They were commissioned on 22 May 2026, ten days before the winter timetable began. From 0.5 nm north of the beacon the array lies behind it within 4 degrees of the same bearing and within 1.5 degrees of the same elevation. It is continuously lit while the beacon flashes green for 0.4 seconds every 2.5 seconds. The Council's planning unit approved the development, and the Port Authority's aids to navigation officer was not consulted. No assessment of the lighting against the channel's aids was made or required.

The master described looking "into a wall of light" and called the beacon "a nothing" against the town and the new car park. The outgoing master independently described the beacon as washed out from the north since the car park lighting was installed. For at least the last 37 seconds before the master called the beacon, it was clear of the islet and not seen. That is the stretch in which the canopy no longer screened the light and the floodlight array lay behind it.

Against this, the beacon was screened by the canopy over most of the search and would not have been visible against a black background either. The heading change began at the plotter before the search, so the floodlights cannot have caused the turn. No measurement exists of what could be seen on the night, only a survey eleven days later. Nothing establishes a detection threshold for a 0.4 second green flash against that background, and the master said the lights might or might not be why the beacon was not seen. The evidence for and against is evenly balanced, and on the evidence available it cannot be determined either way whether the floodlights delayed the sighting in the seconds after the light cleared the islet, and so the moment the held heading was noticed. A measured detection threshold for the flash against the array would settle it, and none is available. The matter is unresolved.

Unresolved: fatigue of the master

On the evidence, whether the master was fatigued during the transit is about as likely as not. The master was on day nine of a twelve-day tour, on a split duty of 05:40 to 08:40 and 13:00 to 19:20 with a 13 hour 40 minute spread, and the channel transit fell in its last hour and a quarter. The master's fatigue diary gave 6 hours 15 minutes of sleep the night before, and in interview the master said "I was tired. I'd be lying if I said otherwise." The misjudgement of distance after the sighting, taking the vessel to be a boat width outside the edge when it was nearly 40 m out, is the kind of error fatigue is expected to produce.

Against this, the master said in the same answer "I wasn't fighting to stay awake and I wasn't slow", and the recorded performance agrees. Helm work held the centreline to within 3 m for the first two minutes in the channel, the response to the shallow alarm took 4 seconds, and the radio work after the grounding was complete and correct at the first attempt. The decision not to refloat was made in about thirty seconds and was right. The master said 6 hours 15 minutes is normal on a split, and nothing else bears on the master's state. The duty was inside the operator's limits and the crewing determination.

No detailed fatigue assessment was made. Each decision that mattered on the night is either accounted for by another factor, such as the missing hold point, or contradicted by the recorded data, so a finding of fatigue would not on this evidence have shown a path to the occurrence that those factors do not already cover. The matter is unresolved.

Other factors that raise risk without having influenced this occurrence

Four further factors passed the test of importance but did not influence this occurrence. The Investigation treated them as contributory factors in the sense that they increased risk.

The Waterways Aids to Navigation Code duties depend on the channel's status, as WAN-2 section 4 sets out under External requirements and agreements. The Merrandi Channel is not a declared shipping channel, so 4.2 did not apply to its beacons, and neither 4.3 nor the services agreement requires availability to be recorded or users to be told of a defect, a deferral or a change. Neither mechanism of 4.2 reaches this occurrence. A notice of the range change would have told the operator about a light that was screened over the stretch where the vessel left the channel, and a better known light is no more visible through a mangrove canopy. An availability figure measures whether a light is lit, and this one was lit throughout. Section 4.1 applies to every aid whatever the channel's status, and what kept WO-118 unfunded was the 50 m vegetation scope of the services agreement. It is unlikely that the code's gap influenced this occurrence, but it is likely to matter as a standing gap in what the users of an undeclared channel are told.

The beacon's conversion from mains to solar in November 2025 halved its nominal range from 6 to 3 nautical miles, and the chart correction lodged on 4 February 2026 was still pending on 7 July 2026. No local notice to mariners was issued and no operator was told. The measured range was 2.6 nm, and the operator's passage plan still gave the beacon at 6 M. The master already knew the light was weaker, saying "It used to be a proper light. It was a mains light." The search ran from 0.47 nm to 0.25 nm, well inside even the measured range, and nothing shows the plan's 6 M figure was used for anything on the night. It is unlikely that the range change influenced the occurrence, because a screened light is not made visible by being brighter. Any effect on conspicuity against the floodlights belongs to the unresolved matter above. It is likely to matter because a master working to the plan on another night would be looking for a light twice as strong as the one present.

The winter roster has the master on that line work the same split of 05:40 to 08:40 and 13:00 to 19:20 on every day of a 12 days on, 2 days off tour, which is 9 hours 20 minutes of duty across a 13 hour 40 minute spread. That is inside the operator's limits of 10 hours of duty and 14 hours of spread but leaves the darkness transit at the end of a spread that closes 20 minutes inside the limit. No relief master is rostered, and the fatigue diary the operator asks masters to keep is not collected. The master had made 26 of the 30 darkness transits before the occurrence. Because the roster's only path to the occurrence is through a fatigue that could not be determined, it is unlikely that the roster influenced this occurrence, and it is likely to matter as a standing exposure on every darkness transit of the timetable.

The forward saloon lifejacket locker holds 40 adult jackets behind the kiosk counter. The survey of 16 July 2026 found that the locker face cannot be reached from 22 of the 34 forward saloon seats without passing behind the counter through a 0.6 m gap, and that the muster placard directs passengers to a locker they cannot see from their seats. The counter was fitted in a 2019 interior refit under a minor modification notice that did not trigger a re-survey. The operator says the same counter is fitted to its two other 24 m vessels. The deckhand had to ask three people at the counter to move and hand jackets over it, and reported at 18:22:40 having had to go round the servery for two passengers. All 38 passengers were in lifejackets by about 18:22 and ashore by 19:26. It is unlikely that the locker influenced the grounding or its outcome, while the risk it represents on a night with a fire, a capsize risk or an injured deckhand is very likely to be significant.

The decision not to refloat

Both engines were stopped 27 seconds after contact and not restarted. The pan pan at 18:13:04 stated "I am not attempting to refloat" as a decision already made. The No. 2 starboard void was sounded and reported at about 75 mm at 18:17:05, and the survey later found a 180 mm split in the starboard hull plating in way of that void, with ingress reaching approximately 260 mm by the time the vessel refloated at 00:20. The master's reasoning, given in interview, was "Falling tide, unknown bottom, thirty eight people aboard". The breach was in the compartment the vessel was sitting on, and refloating it into 3.2 m of water with the ingress unassessed would have put a flooding compartment into deep water with the passengers still aboard. It is very likely that stopping the engines and staying on the bank reduced risk. All 38 passengers were transferred ashore by 19:26 with no serious injury.

Hypotheses considered and not supported

Two hypotheses were tested and not supported. The Port Authority's gauge read 0.91 m at 18:12 against a predicted 0.94 m, and the largest departure from prediction in the twelve hours to 20:00 was 0.07 m. With the bed at the contact point 0.50 m below chart datum there was 1.41 m of water over it against a static draught of 1.35 m and a squat of 0.18 m. At the predicted height the vessel would have touched as well, so the tide set down below prediction is very unlikely. A steering or propulsion failure before the vessel left the centreline is very unlikely, because engine speed, hydraulic pressure and rudder following were steady, the turn was a heading applied and then held, and the tested steering system showed no pre-existing defect. The damage to the starboard shaft, propeller and rudder dated from the contact.

Conclusions

The investigation identified the following causal and contributory factors. They should not be read as apportioning blame or liability to any organisation or individual.

Findings

  1. Work order WO-118, raised in 09/2023 to trim the mangrove canopy on Merrandi Islet, was deferred as unfunded at the 2023, 2024 and 2025 works rounds. It was virtually certain that this happened. It was very likely that it contributed to the occurrence because a trim funded in 2023 would have left the canopy near 3.5 m, under the 4.2 m lantern of the No. 4 beacon.
  1. The No. 4 beacon was not visible from the channel between 0.84 nm and 0.34 nm north of it because the canopy on Merrandi Islet stood in the sightline. It was virtually certain that this was so, and it was likely that it contributed because the one reference that would have shown the held heading was screened while the vessel left the channel.
  1. Route risk assessment RRA-07 issue 2 restricted the Merrandi Channel to daylight transits, and change record CHG-2026-014 moved service TF18 into darkness as a "timetable change only" without reopening it. It was virtually certain that this happened, and it was likely that it contributed because a review would not have closed without a night passage plan.
  1. There was no night passage plan for the Merrandi Channel, no guidance on loss of the plotter during the transit, and no hold point or abort point. It was virtually certain that this was so, and it was very likely that it contributed because nothing in any document prompted the master to stop when the plotter froze.
  1. The operator's defect procedure did not require a fault that had cleared itself to be recorded. It was virtually certain that this was so, and it was likely that it contributed because freezes of the vessel's primary means of position fixing over about a year were never written down and so never reached the firmware fix.
  1. The chart plotter display froze at 18:07:06 and did not recover. It was virtually certain that this happened, and it was very likely that it contributed because the vessel had no position fix of any kind for the following minutes.
  1. The heading eased from 195 to 200 degrees over about a minute from 18:07:06 and was then held, without a decision to turn. It was virtually certain that this happened, and virtually certain that it contributed because it was the only cause of the westing that took the vessel out of the channel.
  1. The transit continued at about eight knots from the plotter freeze until the shallow alarm. It was virtually certain that this happened, and it was very likely that it contributed because a stop begun before about 18:11:40 would have halted the vessel short of the contact point.
  1. The vessel left the dredged channel on its western side at about 18:09:00. It was virtually certain that this happened, and virtually certain that it contributed because the grounding followed directly and only from the vessel being outside the channel.
  1. The echo sounder shallow alarm remained at the 0.9 m setting it was commissioned with in 2019 and gave 16 seconds' warning against a crash stop distance of 92 m. It was virtually certain that this was so, and it was very likely that it contributed because the vessel covered 58 m before contact.
  1. The aids to navigation code applied its availability, recording and notice duties only to aids on a declared shipping channel, and the Merrandi Channel is not one. It was virtually certain that this was so, and unlikely that it contributed to the occurrence. It was likely to be important to safety because no user of the channel was entitled to be told of a change to an aid. (Safety issue)
  1. The No. 4 beacon's nominal range was halved by a solar conversion in 11/2025 and no notice reached the users of the channel. It was virtually certain that this was so, and unlikely that it contributed to the occurrence. It was likely to be important to safety because the operator's passage plan still gave the range as 6 M. (Safety issue)
  1. The winter roster closed a split duty with the darkness transit within 20 minutes of the operator's 14 hour spread limit. It was virtually certain that this was so, and unlikely that it contributed to the occurrence. It was likely to be important to safety because the exposure recurred on every darkness transit. (Safety issue)
  1. On the evidence examined, the forward saloon lifejacket locker was behind the kiosk counter fitted in 2019 without a re-survey of the safety equipment arrangement. It was virtually certain that this was so, and unlikely that it contributed to the occurrence. It was very likely to be important to safety because passengers could not reach the locker without crew help. (Safety issue)
  1. The chart plotter freezes of the morning of 07/07/2026 were passed on verbally at the change of master and not entered in the defect book. It was virtually certain that this happened, and unlikely that it contributed to the occurrence. It was likely to be important to safety because both masters described the same practice.
  1. The master stopped both engines and did not attempt to refloat the vessel on a falling tide. It was virtually certain that this happened, and very likely that it reduced risk because the vessel was holed in the compartment it rested on.
  1. It was very unlikely that the tide was set down below prediction over Boolarong Bank.
  1. It was very unlikely that a steering or propulsion failure preceded the vessel leaving the centreline.

Causal factors

  • Work order WO-118 was deferred as unfunded at three successive works rounds, because the services agreement's 50 m vegetation scope placed work on an islet 240 m from the beacon in the general waterways vote. The canopy grew from 2.1 m in 2019 to 5.8 m, against a lantern height of 4.2 m. It was virtually certain that the deferral occurred. It was very likely that it contributed, because a trim funded at the 2023 round would have kept the beacon open to the channel.
  • The No. 4 beacon was screened by the canopy between 0.84 nm and 0.34 nm north of it. It was virtually certain that this was so. It was likely that it contributed, because the beacon was the only means of fixing left and it was screened while the new heading was held. The heading change began at the plotter before the search started, so the screening did not cause the turn, only its going unnoticed. The beacon was also clear of the islet for at least the last 37 seconds of the search and was still not seen, which limits the weight the screening can bear.
  • The change that moved service TF18 from 16:15 to 17:35 was approved by the Operations Manager on 22/04/2026 as a timetable change only. RRA-07 was not reopened, no night passage plan was written, and the approval of the General Manager Operations that RRA-07 required for a night transit was neither sought nor given. It was virtually certain that this occurred. It was likely that it contributed, because a review would have reached the unlit reach between the No. 2 and No. 4 beacons and could not have closed without a night passage plan. A reopened assessment might have produced a plan with no hold point, so the weight of evidence favours contribution without carrying it further.
  • There was no night passage plan and no hold point for loss of the primary means of position fixing. The plan was written for the daylight transit and stated that night transits were not scheduled. It was virtually certain that this was so. It was very likely that it contributed, because the master had 114 seconds between the freeze and crossing the channel edge, and a named hold point would have applied throughout. A master who did not think of stopping unprompted might not have applied a written rule under the same pressure.
  • OPS-9 did not require a fault that had cleared itself to be recorded, and the plotter was not a statutory item. Freezes over about a year were never written down. It was virtually certain that the procedure had this gap. It was likely that it contributed, because a recorded freeze would have reached the Operations Manager's weekly review and the contractor, who identified the fault as cause code 0x51 against firmware issued in 11/2024. The operator held no subscription to the manufacturer's bulletins, so a recorded freeze might have been reviewed and left, and the speed of any fix could not be established.
  • The chart plotter display froze at 18:07:06 and did not recover. The unit's event log, the bridge audio and the master's account agree. It was virtually certain that this happened. It was very likely that it contributed, because the master worked without the primary means of position fixing from that moment. A 46 hour bench test did not reproduce the fault and found no physical defect, but the contractor identified the cause code as known to the manufacturer and addressed by firmware that had not been applied to this unit.
  • The heading eased from 195 to 200 degrees from the second of the freeze and was held. The rudder followed helm demand within 1.5 degrees, so the turn was steered, and the master said the turn was not a decision. It was virtually certain that this happened. It was virtually certain that it contributed, because with no current and no cross-set at that state of tide it was the only cause of the westing.
  • The transit continued at about eight knots after the freeze. The AIS track recorded 8.4 kt at the freeze and no throttle movement until 18:11:52. The master did not consider stopping, and no lookout was on the bridge. It was virtually certain that this happened. It was very likely that it contributed, because a stop begun before about 18:11:40 would have halted the vessel short of the contact point. Stopping was available from the freeze until then, including the 98 seconds after the master saw the beacon dead ahead.
  • The vessel left the dredged channel on the bank side at about 18:09:00 and was over Boolarong Bank from about 18:11:00. It was virtually certain that this happened. It was virtually certain that it contributed, because the grounding followed directly and only from the vessel being outside the channel.
  • The shallow alarm was set at 0.9 m under the keel, the 2019 commissioning value, and sounded 16 seconds before contact. The vessel covered 58 m in that time against a crash stop figure of 92 m from 8 kt. It was virtually certain that this was so. It was very likely that it contributed, because on a bank gradient of about 1 in 70 the alarm could not have sounded appreciably earlier at that setting. The alarm itself did what it was set to do.

Contributory factors

  • Section 4.2 of the aids to navigation code applied its availability target, its recording duty and its notice to mariners duty only to aids on a declared shipping channel, and the Merrandi Channel is not one. It was virtually certain that this was so. It was unlikely that it contributed to the occurrence, because a notice would not have made a screened light visible and the beacon was lit throughout. It was likely to be important to safety because the operator had no right to be told of a change to a beacon's range, character or position on a channel carrying a 96-passenger ferry in darkness. (Safety issue)
  • The No. 4 beacon was converted to a solar lantern in 11/2025, with a nominal range of 3 nautical miles against 6 for the lantern it replaced, and a measured luminous range of 2.6 nm. The chart correction was still pending on 07/07/2026, no local notice was issued, and the operator's passage plan still gave 6 M. It was virtually certain that this was so. It was unlikely that it contributed to the occurrence, because the beacon was screened where the vessel left the channel, the master already knew the light was weaker, and the search ran well inside the measured range. It was likely to be important to safety because a master working to the plan was looking for a light twice as strong as the one there. (Safety issue)
  • The winter roster put service TF18 at the end of a split duty of 05:40 to 08:40 and 13:00 to 19:20, a spread of 13 hours 40 minutes against a limit of 14 hours, on every day of a 12 days on, 2 days off tour, with no relief master rostered. It was virtually certain that this was so. It was unlikely that it contributed to the occurrence, because the roster reaches it only through fatigue, which the recorded performance did not show. It was likely to be important to safety because the exposure recurred on every darkness transit of the timetable. (Safety issue)
  • On the evidence examined, the forward saloon lifejacket locker was behind the kiosk counter fitted in the 2019 refit under a minor modification notice that did not trigger a re-survey. The locker face could not be reached from 22 of the 34 forward saloon seats without passing behind the counter through a 0.6 m gap, and the operator said the same counter was fitted to its two other 24 m vessels. It was virtually certain that this was so. It was unlikely that it contributed to the occurrence, because the vessel was aground, upright and stable and all 38 passengers were in lifejackets by about 18:22. It was very likely to be important to safety because passengers could not equip themselves without crew help in a different emergency. (Safety issue)
  • The outgoing master told the relieving master at about 13:05 that the plotter had frozen twice that morning, at 10:42 and 11:17, and neither entered it in the defect book. It was virtually certain that this happened. It was unlikely that it contributed to the occurrence, because the freeze at 18:07 was a firmware fault and an entry at 13:05 would have been reviewed only at the end of the week. It was likely to be important to safety because both masters volunteered the same practice, so it was a practice and not a lapse.

Other findings

  • Both engines were stopped 27 seconds after contact and were not restarted, and the pan pan at 18:13:04 stated that the master was not attempting to refloat. The starboard hull was split by 180 mm in way of the No. 2 void, with ingress reaching approximately 260 mm by refloating at 00:20. It was virtually certain that this happened.
